planting.note: Set out container stock in fall in fast-draining, lean soil; propagate new plants from winter stem cuttings since seed is slow and inconsistent without fire-cue treatment.

directions: Native to rocky slopes on Santa Catalina, Santa Cruz, and Santa Rosa Islands, this larger-leaved, tree-like relative of the mainland bush poppy carries glaucous blue-green foliage and a long spring-through-summer parade of glossy four-petaled yellow blooms up to 3 inches across. It wants full sun, lean fast-draining soil, and almost no water once established, tolerating both sandy and clay sites better than many chaparral shrubs. Cut the plant back by roughly half after its main flowering flush to keep growth dense and promote repeat bloom. Propagate from winter stem cuttings under mist, since wild seed germination is tied to fire cues and is unreliable in cultivation.

planting.note: Install from containers in fall so roots establish before the dry season; avoid rich amended soil, which shortens the plant's lifespan.

directions: Endemic to Santa Cruz, Santa Rosa, and Santa Catalina Islands, this mounding subshrub carries narrow, felted gray-green leaves and ball-like umbels of flowers that open whitish to pale pink and age to a rich chocolate-red, remaining attractive as dried seed heads into winter. It thrives in lean, fast-draining soil and full sun with little to no summer water, and is an exceptional butterfly and native-bee plant once established. Avoid heavy soils and overhead irrigation, which invite root rot. Shear lightly after the main bloom cycle to tidy the mound and extend the plant's vigor in the garden.

planting.note: Plant small container stock in fall with minimal root disturbance in gritty, well-drained soil; manzanitas resent transplant shock from larger pots.

directions: This Catalina Island endemic is among the largest and fastest-growing manzanitas, developing into a broad, multi-trunked tree-shrub with smooth reddish bark, oval evergreen leaves, and clusters of white to pale pink urn-shaped winter flowers. It is more forgiving of garden conditions than many manzanitas, tolerating a wider range of soils including clay, but still prefers excellent drainage and infrequent deep watering over supplemental summer irrigation. Sterilize pruning tools between cuts, since manzanitas are prone to a fungal branch dieback that spreads easily on dirty blades. Give it room to develop its sculptural branch structure rather than crowding it among smaller shrubs.

planting.note: Direct-sow fresh acorns in fall immediately after collection since they lose viability quickly; container stock also establishes well if planted before winter rains.

directions: Endemic to Santa Cruz, Santa Rosa, and Santa Catalina Islands, this small, dense-crowned evergreen oak is the dominant oak over large parts of Catalina Island, forming thickets of holly-like spiny leaves that provide excellent wildlife cover and acorns for birds and small mammals. It is slow to moderate in growth, tolerates poor rocky soils and salt-laden coastal wind, and needs no irrigation once established beyond its first couple of seasons. Use it as a dense wildlife hedge, windbreak, or specimen in a coastal native garden where a full-size canopy oak would be too large. Avoid summer water around the root crown to prevent root-rot problems common to California oaks.

planting.note: Set out container plants in fall into lean, well-drained soil on a dry slope; no pretreatment needed for seed, which germinates readily.

directions: This island form of the mainland dune/bluff nightshade, distinguished by its larger, more sprawling habit, is native to rocky canyons and slopes on Santa Catalina Island, producing pale blue-purple, yellow-centered flowers resembling small potato blossoms from spring into summer. It spreads into a loose, wide-arching mound and performs best in dry, rocky, well-drained sites with full sun and no summer irrigation. All plant parts including the black berries are poisonous and should be kept away from children and pets. Cut back old woody growth in late winter to refresh the plant and keep flowering concentrated on newer stems.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall on a well-drained slope in a frost-protected microclimate; occasional deep summer water improves vigor on this one compared to most island chaparral shrubs.

directions: One of only a handful of species in the small family Crossosomataceae, this rare shrub is restricted in California to rocky, volcanic-substrate canyons on Santa Catalina and San Clemente Islands, where it produces solitary white flowers that age to a soft purple tinge from winter through late spring. It prefers full sun to light part shade, sharp drainage, and appreciates occasional deep summer watering more than most island natives, which helps it fill out its naturally sprawling, loosely branched form. It is frost-sensitive and best suited to mild coastal gardens rather than areas with hard freezes. Because it is listed as a California Rare Plant Rank 1B species, gardeners should source plants only from nursery propagation, never wild collection.

planting.note: Set out nursery-propagated container plants in fall in fast-draining sandy soil; seed is scarce and needs about three months of moist cold stratification, so propagation is usually by cuttings instead.

directions: Known from only a handful of wild plants on Santa Cruz Island, this federally endangered barberry has been rescued from near-extinction through propagation at California botanic gardens and is now offered by a small number of native plant nurseries, including Theodore Payne Foundation and Native Sons Wholesale Nursery. Its evergreen, holly-textured leaflets are notably less spiny than most barberries, and clusters of gold-yellow flowers appear from late winter into spring. Grow it in fast-draining sandy soil in coastal sun to light shade with minimal supplemental water once established, since it comes from dry chaparral and coastal scrub on the island. Because wild seed set is poor, most nursery stock is produced from cuttings, and gardeners should treat any plant they grow as a meaningful contribution to the conservation of a critically rare species.
